paper_title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: As LLMs are deployed in increasingly agentic roles (customer support, scheduling, guided troubleshooting, clinical intake), they are implicitly expected to follow structured procedural logic: sequence of prescribed steps that moves conversation from users initial request to completed goal (Guo et al., 2024; Alismail and Lanquillon, 2025). This expectation extends well beyond classical task-oriented dialogues (TOD); it applies to any system where the process of conversation matters as much as its content. The dominant conception of hallucination in LLMs concerns factual errors (Maynez et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025), for instance: confident assertions of incorrect dates, invented product details, or wrong numbers. qualitatively different and practically critical failure mode has, however, received comparatively little attention: an agent that produces entirely truthful, fluent utterances while violating the procedural logic it was instructed to follow. The closest prior notions, hallucination in inter-agent communication (Lin et al., 2025) and faithfulness to grounding knowledge in dialogue (Dziri et al., 2022), concern the accuracy of content, not adherence to conversational process. We call this procedural hallucination: breakdown in process rather than content. procedurally hallucinating agent may skip required steps, pursue different goal than instructed, repeat already-completed actions, or introduce conflicting objectives that derail task completion, all while generating individually plausible responses. Crucially, this failure is orthogonal to factual correctness: no single utterance need be false for the overall conversation to be wrong. Standard hallucination benchmarks (Li et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2022) are blind to such failures because they evaluate the truthfulness of content, not the conversational process. To address this gap, we present DIALFORK, benchmark constructed by forking dialogues at controlled turn positions (Figure 1) to simulate different types of procedural hallucinations. Our main contributions are the following: (a) We define procedural hallucination as phenomenon distinct from factual hallucination, and decompose it into four complementary types grounded in genProcedural adherence and dialogue similarity. parallel line studies whether systems follow prescribed steps, from policy-constrained action sequences (Chen et al., 2021) and procedure-guided action prediction (White et al., 2023) to condition action instruction following (Ghazarian et al., 2025) and workflow generation (Qiao et al., 2025), typically over annotated actions, intents, or slots. Dialogue similarity is largely text similarity: embeddings collapse the turns into one vector (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Zhou et al., 2022) compared by cosine, discarding turn order; TaskDiff (Bhaumik et al., 2023) relies on annotated intents and slots. These benchmark how well models follow procedural instructions; DIALFORK instead benchmarks methods that measure how far conversation deviates from procedure, directly on raw dialogue text, whether an LLM or human produced it.

sections.title: 3.1 Formal Model
sections.content: Most conversational systems do not declare their procedural logic explicitly: states, available actions, and transitions are implicit in the agents instructions, the underlying business process, or the assumed conversational norms. To talk about deviations from this logic precisely, we introduce lightweight abstraction that does not assume any particular implementation. We model the intended logic of conversational agent as tuple = (S, A, δ, O), where is set of conversational states (e.g., steps or phases of the interaction), is set of agent actions (e.g., the communicative functions it can perform), δ : is transition function from the current state and user input to the next state, and is the agents objective. This formulation is intentionally general. It applies to any goal-directed conversational agent. For example, task-oriented dialogue system has the dialogue policy as δ and task completion (e.g., booking hotel room, retrieving balance) as O; medical-intake assistant has clinical protocol as δ and patient triage as O; customer-support agent has troubleshooting procedure as δ and issue resolution as O. conformant dialogue D+ is one whose turns follow W.

sections.title: 4.1 Construction Pipeline
sections.content: STAR as generation basis. We base DIALFORK on STAR (Mosig et al., 2020), which spans 24 tasks across 12 domains (hotel, ride, restaurant, medical, party, spaceship, trivia, weather, etc.). STAR is uniquely suited to our pipeline because its dialogues were originally produced by human role-play: for each dialogue, one human participant was given the system role, with the tasks workflow graph and per-node response templates (Appendix C), and another was given the user role, with persona, task, and goal; the two then conversed in these roles. Crucially, STAR releases not only the resulting dialogues but also these roleplay instructions, exactly as they were given to the two human participants of each dialogue (see Appendix for complete example). We give the same instructions to two LLM agents that take the place of the humans: the system agent receives the instructions given to the human who played the system, and the user agent those given to the human who played the user. To our knowledge, no other public dialogue corpus releases both an explicit workflow for every task, which serves as procedural ground truth, and the instructions given to the humans who produced each conversation. Since every DIALFORK dialogue is newly generated, only STARs instructions and workflows, not its original dialogues, enter the benchmark. Conformant dialogue generation. For each STAR scenario, we use SDIALOG (Burdisso et al., 2026) to run the two agents: the system agent is instructed to follow the workflow faithfully, and the user agent to interact naturally without volunteering all details upfront. Both agents are Gemma4-31B (Google DeepMind, 2026) served locally2; prompts and full implementation details are in Appendix E. The two agents converse until the task is completed or per-task turn budget is reached. After filtering for dialogues that include enough system turns to admit all four fork positions, we retain an initial set of 2,134 valid conformant dialogues. sections.title: 5.1 Task 1: Set-to-Set Distance
sections.content: Consider company that deploys an LLM agent to handle its routine customer requests, or that upgrades its assistant to newer model. Before deployment, it needs to know whether the new agents conversations unfold like the reference ones (e.g., past conversations handled by its human agents or by the previous assistant), and, after deployment, whether they drift over time. Neither question concerns single dialogues; Task 1 captures this setting. Input: two sets of dialogues, reference and target; output: scalar distance between them. To evaluate it with DIALFORK, for each hallucination type and each of the 24 tasks of DIALFORK, we group the forked dialogues by their fork position to obtain four sets Dh (k {1, 2, 3, 4}), and take the set of conformant dialogues for that task, D+, as the reference. Writing µk µ(D+, Dh ) for the distance under set-distance metric µ, we expect the natural procedural-similarity ordering µ1 > µ2 > µ3 > µ4, since earlier forks share less of the conformant prefix and are therefore more procedurally deviant. We report Kendalls τ (Kendall, 1938) between the metric-induced ranking and this ground-truth ordering, averaged across the 24 tasks. Because this ordering follows directly from how forks are constructed, Task 1 also serves as sanity check of DIALFORK itself: if independent metrics recover it, the forked dialogues indeed depart from the conformant ones at their designated positions. sections.content: We define three evaluation tasks on DIALFORK at increasing levels of granularity: set-level, dialoguelevel, and turn-level. The third localizes the deviation, asking where in dialogue hallucination first manifests. sections.title: 5.3 Task 3: Hallucination Turn Prediction
sections.content: Task 3 probes whether method can localize where dialogue first goes off-track, as needed, for instance, by guardrail that monitors live conversation and intervenes as soon as the agent deviates from its intended process. The output is the first turn flagged as off-track, given as its position in the dialogue (counting the turns of both speakers), or none if the dialogue is conformant; for forked dialogues, the goal is to locate the hallucination onset, the fork turn tk, as closely as possible. We consider three regimes of decreasing realism: 1. Streaming: the dialogues turns arrive one at time, and the method must decide after each turn whether the conversation has gone off-track, with no access to future turns, and with no workflow. The most realistic and hardest setting. 2. Non-streaming: the complete dialogue, with no workflow. 3. Non-streaming + workflow: the complete dialogue and its ground-truth workflow, typically unavailable in practice; reported as reference with privileged access to the workflow. sections.title: 6.1 Task 1: Set-to-Set Distance
sections.content: Table 2 reports set-to-set ranking results. Despite relying on different principles (embedding distributions vs. an explicit flow graph), all three distance metrics recover the expected ordering with high agreement (τ 0.88 on average), while lengthonly controls do not. This provides the sanity check announced in 5.1: forks depart from the conformant dialogues at their designated positions, not merely by growing longer. The differences among the three metrics are not statistically significant (see Appendix for the testing protocol): FLOWKL performs on par with FBD and PRD while relying on an interpretable human-readable transition graph. The metrics do differ in which hallucination types they capture best. FLOWKL is the best metric on SSPC, the type that targets step ordering, suggesting that an explicit transition model captures step order better than implicit embedding distributions.

sections.title: 6.2 Task 2: Dialog-to-Dialog Distance
sections.content: Table 3 reports the dialog-to-dialog ranking results across seven encoder families, covering generalpurpose sentence embeddings (SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), LaBSE (Feng et al., 2022), BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024a), Qwen3Embedding (Zhang et al., 2025a), EmbeddingGemma (Vera et al., 2025)) and dialoguespecific embeddings (DSE (Zhou et al., 2022) and D2F (Burdisso et al., 2024)). For each family we report the best-performing variant (checkpoints in Appendix K; per-task results and significance tests in Appendix L). With the baseline methods, the choice of encoder matters: D2F is the best (or tied-best) encoder for Mean, Full, and FLOWDTW. FLOWSCORE, in contrast, is the strongest method for all seven encoders, with statistically significant gains over every other method  (Table 7)  , and lifts all of them above τ =0.81, making results largely independent of the encoder. This supports semantic and procedural similarity being distinct axes: two dialogues can be close in content yet differ in how they unfold. For every encoder, comparing wholedialogue embeddings (Full) ranks forks markedly worse (τ =0.5190.747), since fork and its source largely share their content and thus remain semantically close, whereas matching the same turn embeddings with FLOWSCORE recovers the ordering (0.8120.845). The gap is largest for Qwen3Embedding, strong semantic encoder (0.519 vs. 0.812), and smallest for D2F (0.747 vs. 0.834), the encoder trained to capture dialog flow. None of the controls explains these results. Dialogue length alone is close to chance (Turn-count diff.: τ =0.126). Shared prefix, which reads the fork position off the construction itself, reaches τ =0.682; it is not perfect oracle because replayed prefixes may contain minor rewordings (4). Even so, FLOWSCORE outperforms it for every encoder (p < 0.001), without this construction cue.

sections.title: 6.3 Task 3: Hallucination Turn Prediction
sections.content: Streaming. We report 3-gram language model with LaBSE, the encoder with the best Score (other encoders and : Appendix M). Operating turn by turn and learning only from the train dialogues, the streaming detectors localize the fork within 1.92.2 turns, flagging 9395% of forks at false-alarm rate of 1216%. IT localizes better than SS; NC weighting further sharpens IT (MAE 1.94, the lowest without the ground-truth workflow) and raises coverage, at the cost of more false alarms; plain SS and IT score best (73.69, 73.60). Non-streaming. We prompt five open-weight LLMs (Appendix H). Without the workflow, the zero-shot LLMs localize deviations far less precisely than the streaming detectors (MAE 4.506.48 vs. 1.94) and flag only 7283% of forks, despite seeing the whole dialogue. Given the ground-truth workflow, they localize about as well as the streaming detectors, which can only learn the workflow from past conformant dialogues (here, simulated ones); Llama-3.3-70B localizes best (MAE 1.83) and reaches the best overall Score (77.09, tied with Gemma4-31B), but the LLMs raise more false alarms (1782% vs. 12 16%). These gains, however, require the complete dialogue (deviations surface only after the fact), ideally the workflow, and second LLM supervising the first. The streaming detectors, in contrast, are lightweight, need no workflow specification, and flag deviations as they happen, which makes them promising basis for real-time guardrails. Still, they are simple first baselines, and no method we evaluate exceeds Score of 78 out of 100: the best ones still miss the fork by about two turns and raise false alarms on 1230% of conformant dialogues, so localizing procedural hallucination as it happens remains an open problem. By marking where each dialogue first goes off-track, DIALFORK offers the community testbed to tackle it.

sections.title: 7 Conclusions
sections.content: LLMs deployed in agentic conversational roles can produce individually plausible turns while violating the procedural logic they were meant to follow. We named this failure mode procedural hallucination and introduced DIALFORK, the first benchmark that makes it systematically measurable from raw dialogue text, with construction validated by human judgment, surfacing an axis of conversational quality that existing tools largely miss: procedural similarity, distinct from semantic similarity. Its three tasks open the way to distributional monitoring of agents, procedural retrieval, and real-time guardrails. More broadly, we envision procedural fidelity as first-class property of conversational agents: monitored in deployment, searchable in conversation logs, and ultimately optimized in training, so agents stay on process by design. We release the dataset under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT license.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Single source corpus. DIALFORK is built on STAR, which spans 24 tasks across 12 domains. We chose STAR because, to our knowledge, it is the only public corpus that releases both an explicit workflow for each task and the role-play instructions given to the humans who produced each dialogue, which our pipeline needs to simulate conformant dialogues and to define what counts as deviation; and since all DIALFORK dialogues are newly generated, only STARs metadata, not its original dialogues, enters the benchmark. Still, the empirical results we report are tied to STARs distribution of tasks and domains. The construction pipeline and the formal model make no STARspecific assumptions and apply to any corpus with workflow-level metadata; extending DIALFORK to other corpora (e.g., non-English dialogues, or workflows and domains beyond STARs) as they become available is left to future work and to users of the released generation pipeline. Single-type hallucinations. Each forked dialogue injects exactly one hallucination type at one fork point. Real conversational failures can be compound (multiple types co-occurring) or cascading (one corruption inducing another over subsequent turns). The detectors we propose are not evaluated under such combined conditions, and the four-type taxonomy may need extension to cover them. Simulated rather than observed dialogues. Both conformant and forked dialogues are generated by LLM role-play with single generator (Gemma4-31B) under controlled prompting. The generator only realizes the surface language: the 4https://eloquenceai.eu/ labels come from the construction (seeded replay fixes the prefix, the fork turn, and the fork order), the tasks take only the text as input, and the human study confirms that the generator carries out the injected behavior at the intended turn. Other generators may still produce different language and conversational styles; the released pipeline supports regenerating DIALFORK with any LLM. This gives us scale, reproducibility, and exact groundtruth fork points, but the resulting distribution of language and conversational behavior may differ from dialogues collected from real users and deployed agents. Our human study (Appendix N) shows that the constructed deviations are perceived by people as intended, on five tasks spanning short to long dialogues and different domains; still, methods that work well on DIALFORK may behave differently on naturally-occurring conversations, and conversely. Baseline scope. The methods we report are intended as initial baselines, not as the strongest possible detectors. The streaming detectors use simple -gram models over discrete nodes with no neural training beyond the pretrained encoder; the nonstreaming detectors use zero-shot prompting of five open-weight LLMs without fine-tuning, few-shot examples, or chain-of-thought elicitation. Substantially stronger detectors are likely possible on all three tasks, and we hope users of DIALFORK will explore them. One family is excluded by design: detectors relying on signals internal to the generator (e.g., per-turn likelihood or confidence), which would tie results to one model and do not exist for dialogues produced by other systems or by humans, whereas DIALFORK evaluates methods on text alone.

sections.title: 8 Ethical Considerations
sections.content: DIALFORK is constructed entirely from synthetically generated dialogues; no real user data or personal information is involved. The human study that validates its construction (Appendix N) was carried out by volunteers, participating freely and without financial compensation, who judged only these synthetic dialogues: each participant read and accepted consent statement before starting, could stop at any time, and chose whether to be acknowledged by name or to remain anonymous; the released judgments identify participants only by opaque identifiers. Two further points warrant note. Since the dialogues are produced by an LLM, they may reflect biases present in the generator, and the 24 service-oriented tasks are not necessarily representative sample of real-world conversational settings; results on DIALFORK should be read as evidence about procedural deviation under controlled conditions rather than as direct estimates of deployed-system behavior. In particular, detectors validated on DIALFORK should not be deployed as guardrails in high-stakes settings (e.g., clinical intake) without domain-specific validation, where missed deviations or excessive false alarms carry real costs. We judge the value of an openly available, reproducible benchmark to outweigh this risk, particularly because the same machinery enables the detection, guardrail, and monitoring directions the work is intended to support. The DIALFORK dataset is released under CC BY 4.0 and all accompanying code under the MIT license; their intended use is research on conversational reliability, consistent with these licenses. Use of AI assistants. We used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with writing and editing the paper and helping us with development of the annotation tool used in the human study (Appendix N). All AIassisted text and code were reviewed, edited, and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content.

Coverage varies substantially across tasks, reflecting both the heterogeneous yield of valid conformant generations and the variable workflow complexity inherited from STAR; per-task dialogue lengths span more than 2 (from 12.41 turns for ride_status to 29.28 for trivia). Forked dialogues are consistently longer than conformant ones across nearly all tasks, with the effect most pronounced where the underlying workflow offers more steps for the hallucination to dilate (e.g., trivia: 19.45 conformant vs. 29.90 forked mean turns). A.1 Task 3 Train/Test Split In Tasks 1 and 2, conformant dialogues are only used as reference: each fork is compared with its conformant dialogue, and the conformant dialogues themselves are never scored. These two tasks therefore do not need train and test set, and they use all the dialogues of DIALFORK. Task 3 is different. Here, conformant dialogues are also scored, since method should not raise an alarm on them. At the same time, Task 3 method is allowed to learn from conformant dialogues. This matches how such detector would be used in practice: the past conversations of an agent show how it behaves when it follows its workflow, but its future mistakes are not known in advance. The streaming detectors, for example, learn their flow graph, their -gram model, and their thresholds from conformant dialogues. If method were then scored on the same conformant dialogues it learned from, its results would look better than they really are. For this reason, DIALFORK defines train set and test set for Task 3. How we build them. We first divide the 2,134 conformant dialogues into two groups of about the same size. This is done separately for each task: the conformant dialogues of the task are shuffled with fixed seed, and half of them go to the test group (one more if their number is odd). Each fork always goes to the same group as the conformant dialogue it comes from. This is important because fork repeats its conformant dialogue up to the fork turn; if the two were in different groups, test fork would start with the same turns as dialogue used for training. Thanks to this procedure, every task appears in both groups, and every hallucination type and fork position is equally represented. The train set contains only the conformant dialogues of the first group: 1,061 dialogues. These are the only dialogues method may learn from. The smallest task, ride_status, has 4 of them. The test set contains all the dialogues of the secits 1,073 conformant dialogues and ond group: their 17,168 forks, that is, 18,241 dialogues. Every method is scored on all of them. Table 6 gives the size of the train and test sets for each task. What about the forks of the first group? They are included in the released dataset, with their labels, like all other forks, but they are not part of the train set, and we do not use them in this paper. method that learned from them would learn from examples of hallucinations whose position and content were decided by our construction: for instance, forks happen at evenly spaced positions, and the injected behaviors come from small, fixed set. real deployment offers neither of these. If method does use these forks, its results should be reported as different setting, and not compared directly with the ones in this paper. Our experiments. All Task 3 results in this paper are computed on the test set. Only the streaming detectors learn from the train set; the LLMs are used zero-shot, and the trivial baselines do not learn anything. The train and test sets are released with DIALFORK, and the evaluation script scores the test set by default.

sections.title: C STAR Workflow Example
sections.content: To make the role of STARs workflow metadata concrete, we show the doctor_schedule task in full. STAR provides each task as JSON object containing directed graph of conversational states (graph) and template utterance for each state (replies). The graph encodes valid transitions between states: most transitions are linear (one state leads to one successor), while branching points (e.g., available/unavailable, yes/no) represent decisions conditioned on the users response or database query. The replies field associates each state with natural-language template that the system agent uses, as an example, to phrase its turn at that state. sections.title: E Generation Details
sections.content: Implementation is based on SDIALOG,5 modular toolkit that exposes abstractions for agent personas, turn-level orchestration, and scenario management, simplifying the seed-controlled forking pipeline at the heart of DIALFORKs construction. Implementation design in SDialog classes. The generation pipeline is organized around four SDialog abstractions: Agent: one System agent and one User agent are instantiated per scenario. Dialog: stores each generated conversation (conformant and injected variants with all relevant metadata). HallucinationOrchestrator: custom orchestrator attached to the System Agent to manipulate its behavior in real time during generation. LengthOrchestrator: attached to both agents to keep dialogue length within pertask turn budget (see below). Conformant generation setup. Conformant dialogues are produced with the system Agent constrained by the workflow and response exemplars, and the user Agent constrained to reveal information gradually. The user and system agent prompts are reproduced in Listings 4 and 5. Dialogue length is controlled with SDIALOGs LengthOrchestrator: once dialogue reaches per-task turn budget, set to the maximum length of the corresponding STAR tasks human dialogues, both agents are nudged to wrap up the conversation, with hard cutoff five turns later. The same budget and orchestration apply to conformant dialogue and to all of its forks, so their lengths are bounded identically, although not matched dialogue by dialogue (forked dialogues remain longer on average; Figure 4). Generator choice, decoding, and compute. The generator was selected after manually inspecting pilot dialogues from several open-weight LLMs (Gemma3 and 4, Qwen2.5, 3, and 3.6, Phi4, DeepSeek-R1, Nemotron-3-Nano, Llama3.1) and from GPT-4.1 as closed-source reference. Both agents run Gemma4-31B served locally with Ollama, 5https://github.com/idiap/sdialog one NVIDIA V100 GPU per generation job, with temperature 1.3 for diversity and top-p 0.95 and topk 64 (the models recommended values); degenerate outputs (e.g., repetition loops) are detected and retried (see below). Generating dialogue takes 83 on average, and the full dataset (36,278 dialogues, about 750K turns and 10.4M words) about 33 GPU-days in total. Custom orchestrator used for hallucination injection. Hallucination injection is implemented with custom HallucinationOrchestrator subclassing SDialogs BaseOrchestrator. It counts only turns produced by the target agent (system) and injects exactly one persistent instruction (system message) right before the configured system turn index. The injected message is composed as general hallucination instruction template (Listing 6) containing one type-specific hallucination template (see F). Determinism and injection timing. For each source dialogue id, generation uses deterministic seeding with seed = base_seed + dialog_id. Injection turns are computed from the number of system turns in the conformant dialogue and spaced over segments using: tk = 1+round (cid:18) (k 1) Tsys (cid:19) , = 1, . . . , K. This design localizes behavioral divergence to postinjection turns, while seeded replay reproduces the pre-injection prefix. Variant sampling and references. To increase diversity and controllability, at injection time, each hallucination type template (F) is instantiated by sampling one goal/policy and effect from its variants described in Appendix B. Step-policy, goalreplacement, and conflicting-constraint families are sampled from fixed variant sets; workflow-identity corruption samples workflow from different task within the same domain. Quality checks, retries, and output bookkeeping. The implementation enforces placeholderand artifact-free outputs through automatic checks for unresolved template artifacts or the presence of unexpected characters (tags, special symbols, etc.). Failed generations are retried with new random seeds up to fixed retry budget; unresolved cases are excluded. Additionally, only dialogues with at least 5 (i.e., number of forks + 1) system turns are eligible for injection, preventing degenerate cases where the trigger occurs at or beyond termination. Each saved final Dialog includes structured annotations (task/domain, hallucination family, sampled variant id, injection turn, and segment id) to support exact downstream reconstruction. System and user prompt fields. The domains, scenario_description, and flowchart_info placeholders are populated from the original STAR workflow and role-play metadata (Appendices and D). sections.content: DIALFORKs ground truth comes from its construction: each forked dialogue carries the hallucination type and variant that was injected, the fork turn tk at which it was injected, and its fork position relative to the other forks of the same conformant dialogue. This appendix describes the human study we use to validate these labels, and to compare the automatic metrics of 5 with human judgments of procedural conformance. Results are summarized in 4 and reported in detail in N.7. N.1 Research Questions The study is designed around four research questions, summarized in Table 10, each targeting one label or claim that the benchmark relies on. We additionally relate the automatic distances of Task 2 to the human judgments (N.6). RQ1 (Fork order). Does fork position track the degree of procedural deviation perceived by humans? If forking works as intended, dialogues forked later, which follow the intended workflow for longer, should be judged more conformant than dialogues forked earlier, and conformant dialogues the most conformant of all. This is the ordering that Tasks 1 and 2 use as ground truth. RQ2 (Injection validity). Does the injected behavior actually appear in the forked dialogue? This validates the hallucination type and variant labels, per type. RQ3 (Localization). Does the deviation start at the intended fork turn? This validates tk, the ground truth of Task 3. RQ4 (Prefix conformance). Before the fork, does the assistant follow the intended workflow? This validates that the replayed prefix is generated under the intended policy (4). N.2 Participants Thirty-one volunteers were recruited, colleagues from our institutions and external participants, none of whom took part in building the dataset. Each annotator was assigned number of conversations matching their initial time availability, from 5 to 60 (at an estimated 2.5 minutes each), and several asked for more once they had finished. Conversations are assigned in batches drawn from single STAR task, so that all the conversations in batch follow the same workflow. We assigned most annotators single task, so that they could become familiar with one workflow rather than relearn new one every few conversations; only those with larger loads worked on two or three tasks. Since participation was voluntary, annotators could stop at any time. Annotators accessed the study through personal link, read and accepted consent statement before starting, and are identified only by an opaque identifier in the collected data; each could choose to be acknowledged by name in the final version of the paper or to remain anonymous. N.3 Sample We selected five tasks spanning short to long weather, dialogues and different domains: plane_book, bank_fraud_report, hotel_book, and party_plan. Conversations are drawn in miniblocks of five: four forked dialogues forming one row of type fork-position Latin square (each hallucination type once and each fork position once) plus one conformant dialogue. Annotators receive their conversations one mini-block at time, shuffled within each block, so whatever an annotator completes is balanced on hallucination type and fork position even if they stop early. No annotator ever sees two versions of the same source dialogue: all versions share the same opening, so seeing two of them would let an annotator compare them directly instead of judging each one against the workflow. For the same reason, we collect independent ratings rather than asking annotators to rank the four forks of dialogue side by side: such ranking could be read off the length of the shared opening, the very construction cue the study must look past. The ranking is instead recovered from independent ratings, across annotators (N.6). Sample size. The study samples the construction procedure rather than the dataset: every forked dialogue is produced by the same pipeline, prompts, and generator, so the conversations we annotate are exchangeable draws from it, and the number needed depends on the precision sought, not on the size of DIALFORK. About 380 conversations bound the 95% margin of error of any overall rate by 5 points, whatever the rate, even after the finite-population correction for the 36,278 dialogues of DIALFORK. We therefore planned 500 conversations, together with set judged by two or three annotators to measure agreement. Final sample. Of the 31 volunteers recruited, one never started, so 30 annotators took part, and four of them stopped before completing their assignment, which voluntary participation allows; since Table 10: Research questions of the human study, the label or claim each one validates, how it is measured (step of the annotation item, N.4), the statistic reported, and the result (N.7).

The final sample comprises 428 conversations, still above the 380 required: 342 forked dialogues (85 or 86 per hallucination type and per fork position) and 86 conformant ones, with 526 judgments in total, about 12.6 hours of annotation. Seventy conversations are judged by two (42) or three (28) annotators and are used to measure inter-annotator agreement. N.4 Annotation Protocol Learning the task. Before their first conversation, annotators see short introduction to their task: one-line description of the systems goal and its workflow, written as numbered steps in plain language (e.g., Ask which doctor they want to see), with each branch nested under the step it comes from (e.g., If it is not available . . . ) and the STAR response template of each step available as an example on demand. The original STAR flowchart is also shown. The same workflow panel stays visible next to every conversation (Figure 7). Annotators are told that only the assistant is judged, and that the exact wording of its turns does not matter, only the steps it performs. Three steps per conversation. Each conversation is annotated in three steps, always in the same order, and an answer cannot be changed once the next step is shown. The order is what keeps each answer independent of the information revealed afterwards: 1. Overall conformance (RQ1). The assistant was told to follow the steps on the left. How well does it?, answered on 0100 slider (0: ignores them; 100: follows them). Nothing about the conversations construction has been revealed at this point, so this judgment is blind to the hallucination type, the fork position, and whether the conversation was forked at all. 2. Cued check (RQ2, RQ3). Annotators are told that at some point, the assistant was given an extra instruction and what it was meant to do from then on (e.g., Choose actions inconsistently so the dialogue appears chaotic and disconnected from the intended flow; for WIC, the description of the substitute task), and asked Does that happen in this conversation? (yes / partly / no). If yes or partly, they click the first assistant turn where it starts to happen. The fork turn is not marked at this point. 3. Prefix check (RQ4). Annotators judge whether, before the fork, the assistant follows the steps (yes / mostly / no). To delimit this part, the fork region is highlighted, and the injected instruction is shown next to the annotators step-2 answer, without any score or evaluative feedback. Annotators can also leave free-text note. The question is skipped when there is no prefork part (conformant dialogues and forks with tk = 1). Foils. cued question alone could be answered yes indiscriminately. To measure this, every conformant dialogue and about 20% of the forked dialogues are shown foil in step 2: the description of variant from different hallucination type, which never occurs in that conversation, so the correct answer is no. Foils are assigned deterministically per conversation, independently of the annotator. The difference between the confirmation rate of true instructions and that of foils is what separates genuine detection from acquiescence. Feedback and learning. Because annotators see the injected instruction and the true fork turn after each conversation (step 3), they could in principle learn regularities of the construction over time. We therefore report onset accuracy and foil confirmation separately for the first, middle, and last third of each annotators sequence (N.7). N.5 Annotation Tool We built dedicated web application for the study (Figure 7), which we release together with the DIALFORK dataset and source code, along with the anonymized judgments collected in this study. It is implemented in Python with no third-party dependencies, opens the dataset read-only, and stores all answers in single SQLite database. Annotator interface. The annotator view shows the workflow steps on the left and the conversation on the right, with the assistant turns emphasized and numbered and the user turns in muted style; the current step is shown in panel at the bottom (Figure 7ac). Progress is shown per task. Blinding is enforced by the server. The browser never receives information ahead of the step that needs it: the step-1 payload contains no cue and no fork turn, the step-2 payload contains the cue but not the fork turn, and step cannot be requested before the previous one has been submitted. Conversations are identified in the browser by opaque random tokens, so neither the hallucination type nor the fork position can be inferred from them. Presentation order and foil assignment are randomized server-side with stored seeds, so every presentation can be reconstructed. Administrator interface. An administrator panel, protected by password, is used to create annotators (each receiving personal link), draw batches of conversations for given task following the sampling rules above, assign them, and monitor progress (Figure 7d). It also recomputes all the analyses below from the answers collected so far and exports the raw answers. N.6 Analysis Aggregation. Categorical answers (steps 2 and 3) use the first judgment collected for each conversation, so that each conversation counts once; the slider uses the mean over the annotators who judged the conversation. Agreement is computed only on the conversations judged by more than one annotator. RQ1: fork order. Our primary statistic is computed within each (annotator, task) pair: Kendalls τb (Kendall, 1938) between the annotators slider values and the fork positions of the forked dialogues they judged, which removes differences in how individual annotators use the scale. We average τb over all pairs with at least eight forked dialogues covering all four positions, and report bootstrap confidence interval (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993). To make the effect size directly interpretable, we also report the probability of superiority (McGraw and Wong, 1992): among pairs of conversations judged by the same annotator within the same task and at different positions, the share in which the later one is rated higher (ties count one half; chance is 50%), with bootstrap confidence interval over (annotator, task) pairs, and with conformant dialogues counted as the latest position. As the closest analogue of Task 2, we also compute τb within each quartet, the four forks of the same source dialogue under the same hallucination type; since no annotator sees two versions of the same source dialogue, the four forks of quartet are necessarily judged by four different annotators. As an anchor, conformant dialogues should receive the highest scores. Since the step-1 question asks how well the assistant follows the workflows steps, and CSC is the only hallucination type that keeps every component of the workflow, adding competing objective on top  (Table 1)  , we report these statistics over the three types that break component of the workflow (WIC, SSPC, and GR), and, for completeness, over all forks. We also report mean slider values per fork position, overall and per hallucination type (a within-annotator τb per type would need each annotator to judge every type at every fork position, which only the largest loads cover). RQ2RQ4. We report confirmation and conformance rates with Wilson confidence intervals (Wilson, 1927): for RQ2, per hallucination type and against foils; for RQ4, per fork position. For RQ3, (a) Step 1: overall conformance, before any cue. (b) Step 2: the cued check (here, an SSPC instruction). (c) Step 3: the prefix check. (d) Administrator panel: annotators, batches. links, progress, and Figure 7: The annotation tool, shown on demonstration instance with placeholder annotators (doctor_schedule task). The workflow steps stay visible on the left of every conversation; only the assistant turns are judged. we report the distribution of the difference between the annotated onset and tk, and the share of exact and within-one-turn matches. Reliability. On the doubly-judged conversations, we report raw agreement and Gwets AC1 (Gwet, 2008) for the categorical answers, and Krippendorffs α (Krippendorff, 2004) (interval) for the slider and the onset turn. We report AC1 rather than Cohens or Fleiss κ as the primary agreement statistic because the confirmation question is expected to be heavily skewed, setting in which κ is known to be low even under high agreement (Feinstein and Cicchetti, 1990). Each annotators foil false-confirmation rate, i.e., how often they confirmed an instruction that was never injected, provides an objective per-annotator reliability measure that requires no comparison between annotators; it is the only criterion we use to exclude an annotator, and any exclusion is reported. Since foil shown on forked dialogue can partly match the deviation that the dialogue does contain, the criterion uses only the foils shown on conformant dialogues, for which the correct answer is unambiguously no: an annotator is excluded if they confirm more than half of them, i.e., if they report an injected behavior in conversation where none was injected more often than not. The criterion is applied to annotators shown at least two conformant dialogues; those who judged single mini-block see only one, which is too few to assess. Secondary: relation to automatic metrics. Beyond the four research questions, for each forked dialogue D, we compute its distance to its conformant original, µ(D+, D), under each Task-2 method and each length-only control, and report Spearmans ρ (Spearman, 1904) between this distance and the human-perceived deviation (100 minus the mean slider), with bootstrap confidence intervals. Note that this analysis answers different question from Task 2: Task 2 ranks the four forks of the same conformant dialogue under the same hallucination type, whereas here dialogues from different sources, tasks, and hallucination types are pooled, so the correlation also reflects how each method weighs the different types of deviation. Figure 8: Human study results, one panel per research question. (a) RQ1: mean step-1 conformance rating per fork position over WIC, SSPC, and GR forks (bars) and over all four types (markers; CSC keeps every component of the workflow, see text), and for conformant dialogues, with 95% bootstrap CIs. (b) RQ2: share of forked dialogues in which the true injected instruction was confirmed (yes or partly), per hallucination type, vs. the share of foil instructions confirmed, with 95% Wilson CIs. (c) RQ3: absolute difference between the annotated onset and the fork turn tk, over confirmed true instructions. (d) RQ4: answers to the prefix question per fork position (k=1 forks have no pre-fork part). N.7 Results Figure 8 summarizes the results, one panel per research question. The median time per conversation, all three steps included, was 1.4 minutes. RQ1: fork order. Step 1 asks how well the assistant follows the workflows steps. CSC is the only hallucination type that keeps every component of the workflow, including its goal, and adds competing objective on top  (Table 1)  ; its forks are clearly perceived as deviating, rated below conformant dialogue by the same annotator in 87% of pairs [80, 93] and with the injected behavior confirmed in 88% of them (RQ2), but the degree of deviation perceived on this question changes little with fork position (from 59 at k=1 to 70 at k=4), as the added constraint shows in the same way whenever it is injected. Over the three types that break component of the workflow (WIC, SSPC, and GR; Figure 8a, bars), perceived conformance increases with every fork position, from 14/100 at k=1 and 19 at k=2 to 41 at k=3 and 58 at k=4, with conformant dialogues rated highest (94). Compared within the same annotator and task, later fork is rated above an earlier one in 80% of pairs (95% CI [76, 84]; chance is 50%), fork at k=4 above one at k=1 in 90% [83, 96], and conformant dialogue above forked one in 96% [94, 98]. The corresponding rank correlation is strong, with mean τb of 0.57 [0.50, 0.63] (p < 0.001, one-sided Wilcoxon test against 0); note that with four forks at each position, ties in cap τb at about 0.89 even for perfectly ordered annotator. In the setting that mirrors Task 2, the four forks of the same source dialogue under the same hallucination type, the correlation is stronger still, with τb reaching 0.64 [0.43, 0.80] over 23 quartets (p < 0.001), even though each quartet mixes the rating scales of four different annotators. As an anchor, conformant dialogues are rated highest for every (annotator, task) pair. For each of these three types, forks at k=4 are rated well above forks at k=1 (GR 3 vs. 52, SSPC 12 vs. 62, WIC 24 vs. 61), and for GR the rating rises at every step (3, 16, 27, 52). The first two positions are the closest: t1 and t2 are on average fewer than two assistant turns apart, and these opening turns (e.g., greeting the user, asking for their name) are largely generic. Including CSC (Figure 8a, markers), the ordering holds as well: ratings rise from 26 at k=1 and 27 at k=2 to 47 at k=3 and 61 at k=4; later fork is rated above an earlier one in 72% of pairs [68, 75], fork at k=4 above one at k=1 in 82% [76, 88], and conformant dialogue above forked one in 94% [91, 96]; the rank correlation is moderate, with τb of 0.41 [0.35, 0.48] within annotators and 0.45 [0.25, 0.64] over 33 quartets (both < 0.001); and conformant dialogues are rated highest for 88% of the (annotator, task) pairs. RQ2: injection validity. Told which instruction had been injected, annotators confirmed that it is carried out in 91% of forked dialogues (95% CI [86, 94]; yes in 80%, partly in 11%), and in at least 87% for every hallucination type, from WIC (87%) to GR (96%) (Figure 8b). Foils, which describe behavior that was never injected, were confirmed far less often: in 8% of conformant dialogues (p < 0.001, one-sided Fisher exact test). On forked dialogues, which do deviate from the workflow, description of different deviation can partly match the one that is present, and foils were confirmed in 45% of cases; the true instruction was still confirmed twice as often (91%, < 0.001), showing that annotators recognize the specific injected behavior and not merely that something went wrong. RQ3: localization. Annotators placed the onset of the injected behavior, the quantity that Task 3 predicts, exactly at the fork turn tk in 67% of confirmed forks (median error 0 turns) and within one turn of it in 77% (Figure 8c). Deviations from tk are almost always late: 96% of onsets are at or after tk, consistent with an injected instruction sometimes taking turn or two to become visible when the next steps are shared by the intended and the injected behavior (e.g., WIC substitute task that, like the intended one, starts by identifying the user). Annotators also agree closely with one another on the onset (Krippendorffs α = 0.84, above the 0.8 reliability threshold; see Agreement below). RQ4: prefix conformance. For forks with prefork part (tk > 1), annotators judged that the assistant followed the workflow before the fork in 86% of cases and mostly followed it in further 9% (95% combined, 95% CI [91, 97]), with the same share of yes at every fork position (8586%; Figure 8d). This confirms that seeded replay generates the prefix under the intended policy. Agreement. On the conversations judged by more than one annotator, agreement on whether the injected instruction is carried out (yes or partly vs. no, the RQ2 measure) is 0.83, substantial agreement (AC1 = 0.69; Landis and Koch, 1977); most disagreements are between yes and partly (three-way agreement 0.68, AC1 = 0.54). Agreement on the prefix question is almost perfect (raw 0.87, AC1 = 0.85). For the continuous answers, Krippendorffs α is high for the onset turn (0.84, above the 0.8 threshold for reliable data; Krippendorff, 2004), with 88% of annotator pairs within one turn of each other, and 0.66 for the conformance slider. Learning across the sequence. We find no sign that annotators learned regularities of the construction from the feedback shown after each conversation (N.4). Splitting each annotators sequence into first, middle, and last thirds, onset accuracy does not increase towards the end (within one turn: 77%, 84%, 76%; highest in the middle third), and neither does the confirmation of true instructions (92%, 86%, 96%), while foil confirmation decreases (33%, 22%, 17%): over time, annotators became, if anything, more careful in rejecting instructions that were not carried out, not more inclined to confirm them. Reliability and scale use. No annotator met the exclusion criterion (N.6), so all judgments are kept. One annotator used the slider in binary way (almost exclusively 0 or 100), judging whether the assistant followed the workflow rather than how closely. Excluding them leaves the mean ratings per fork position within 3 points and the mean τb over all forks at 0.43 (vs. 0.41), so we report all annotators. relation to automatic metrics. Secondary: Over the annotated forks, every embedding-based Task-2 distance correlates moderately to strongly with human-perceived deviation (Spearman ρ from 0.58 for FLOWSCORE to 0.67 for Mean-turn), well above the weak correlation of the length-only controls (0.360.37). This is consistent with RQ1: perceived deviation depends on the fork position, but also on the hallucination type and on the particular conversation (e.g., CSC forks are perceived as the mildest deviation at every position), and distance computed on each dialogue can reflect these differences too. As this analysis pools dialogues across sources, tasks, and types (N.6), it does not rank the methods on Task 2. sections.content: The study covers 428 conversations from five tasks. To extend its checks to the whole corpus, every dialogue of the 24 tasks, we use the human judgments to calibrate an LLM judge, and apply the judge to the whole corpus as an additional sanity check of the construction. The judge is an instrument calibrated against people, not second ground truth: the labels remain those of the construction. Judge. The judge sees what the annotators saw (the workflow as numbered steps, the users goal, and the transcript with numbered assistant turns) and answers the three questions of N.4 in the same order, one at time within single chat, with the same cues and foils. We compared 13 judges: five open-weight LLMs (Gemma4-31B, Qwen3.6-35B, GPT-OSS-20B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B (Mistral AI, 2025) and Llama-3.3-70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024)), each with the annotators wording and with added rubric anchors, and the three that support it also with reasoning enabled, all served with Ollama and greedy decoding. We selected the judge on three of the five tasks (hotel_book, bank_fraud_report, weather) by its mean agreement with the annotators (AC1 on confirmation, Krippendorffs α on the rating and on the onset turn), froze it, and evaluated it on the other two (plane_book, party_plan), whose workflows it had not seen. To avoid self-verification, we excluded the generator, Gemma4-31B, although with reasoning enabled it was the best judge on the selection tasks. The selected judge is Qwen3.6-35B with the annotators wording. Agreement with people. On the 25 held-out conversations judged by several annotators, the judge agrees with each annotator about as well as two annotators agree with each other: AC1 0.71 against 0.59 on confirmation, α 0.70 against 0.48 on the rating, and 0.82 against 0.89 on the onset turn. With so few conversations the intervals are wide (the annotator-to-annotator AC1 on confirmation has 95% CI of [0.28, 0.86]), so we read this as agreement within the range of human agreement, not above it. Whole corpus. Table 11 compares the judge with the annotators on the studys conversations, and reports it on all dialogues. On the whole corpus, the judge reproduces the four findings of the study: ratings rise with the fork position and are highest
